questions_asked: In Washington, when the public reports a suspected Asian giant hornet, what is the agency's usual first step to check the report?
Among Washington reports of an Asian giant hornet that turn out to be false, which insects are mistaken most often?
When you see a report with a clear close-up photo or a captured specimen, how much does that raise your confidence it is really a giant hornet?
Do false reports about giant hornets show a pattern by month or season? If so, roughly what pattern?
Do false reports concentrate in certain kinds of places, like farms, gardens, or suburbs? Any clear pattern?
Do false reports cluster near real confirmed hornet sightings? Why might that happen?
How long does the agency typically wait after a confirmed hornet sighting before sending crews back to recheck the area?
What would convincing evidence be that the giant hornet is truly gone from Washington? How long would that take to say?
When you hear new hornet reports piling up over time, at what point does it feel like a real spread, not just noise?
How many field visits can the agency realistically send out per week to follow up on reports?
expert_answers: The usual first step is a desk review of the report by state entomology staff: they look at the submitted photo(s) or video and the reporter's notes/description, and compare them against the known appearance of *Vespa mandarinia* (large size, orange-and-black head, distinct abdominal banding) versus common look-alikes. This triage is done remotely, without a field visit, and is what produces the "Negative ID" or "Unprocessed/Unverified" lab status in the dataset. Only reports that survive this screening — or that come with strong evidence (a specimen, clear close-up image, or a report from a trained observer) — trigger the next step, which is a follow-up contact with the reporter and, if warranted, a site visit or trap placement.

The most common false reports are other large wasps and hornets — especially the **European hornet** (*Vespa crabro*) and **yellowjackets/bald-faced hornets** (*Dolichovespula maculata*), plus **paper wasps**. Also frequent: **bumble bees** (large, fuzzy, black-and-yellow), **carpenter bees**, and large **hover flies** (which mimic wasps). The state's own lab comments in the dataset typically name these groups. This is an empirical judgment based on the look-alike literature and the dataset's Lab Comments, not a precise count.

A clear close-up photo or a captured specimen raises confidence substantially — it is the single strongest evidence short of a confirmed nest. With a good close-up showing the diagnostic features (large size, orange-and-black head, distinct abdominal banding), a trained reviewer can often make a near-definitive call; a physical specimen is essentially confirmatory. By contrast, distant or blurry photos, or reports with only a text description, remain weak evidence because the common look-alikes (European hornet, yellowjackets, bumble bees) are easily confused at a distance. So the presence of a clear image or specimen typically moves a report from "possible" to "highly likely," and is the main trigger for escalation to a site visit. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise probability.

Yes. False reports follow a strong seasonal pattern driven by insect activity and public attention, peaking in late summer and early fall (roughly August–October), when wasp and hornet colonies are largest, workers are most visible foraging, and queens are active. A secondary, smaller rise occurs in spring (April–June) as overwintering queens emerge and people start noticing large insects. Reports are lowest in winter (December–February), when almost no wasps are flying and public attention fades.

This is an empirical judgment based on wasp phenology and the timing of the Washington reports, not a precise count. The pattern is a seasonal cycle, not a monotonic trend, so any model should treat month/season as a categorical or cyclical feature rather than a linear one.

Yes, there is a clear pattern, and it is driven mainly by where people are and where flowering/insect-attracting habitat is.

False reports concentrate in **residential and suburban areas** — yards, gardens, porches, decks, and parks — because that is where most people encounter large flying insects and where ornamental flowers, fruit trees, and gardens attract wasps, bees, and hover flies. **Rural/farm and agricultural land** also produces a meaningful share, tied to orchards, crops, and apiaries, but the volume is lower simply because fewer people are there to report.

The key point is that this is largely a **reporting-effort / observer-density pattern**, not a true hornet-habitat pattern: false reports cluster wherever human population density is high and outdoor activity is common. So location type is informative mostly as a proxy for how many people are looking, and any spatial model should account for population density rather than treating "suburb" as intrinsically hornet-prone. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise count.

Yes, they do cluster near confirmed sightings, and this is one of the more reliable spatial patterns in the data.

Two mechanisms drive it:

1. **Attention/awareness spillover.** After a confirmed detection is publicized, people in the surrounding area become primed to notice and report large insects. Reporting effort rises locally, so false reports rise too — the same observer-density effect as before, but concentrated around the news.

2. **Genuine look-alike co-occurrence.** Confirmed hornet areas are also areas with wasps, yellowjackets, and other large insects, so the same habitat that produces a real detection produces plausible false reports nearby.

The practical consequence: proximity to a confirmed sighting is informative but **confounded** — it raises the prior that a report is real, yet it also inflates the local volume of false reports. So a spatial model should treat "distance to nearest confirmed detection" as a feature while controlling for local reporting effort/population density, not as a standalone signal. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise count.

There is no fixed waiting interval. In practice, after a confirmed detection the agency does not "wait and recheck" on a set clock — it acts within days to about a week or two, because the priority is to find and destroy the nest before new queens emerge (fall) or before the colony expands (spring/summer).

The follow-up is typically: immediate intensified trapping and visual surveys in a roughly 1–5 km radius around the confirmation, repeated through the active season (roughly through October), rather than a single delayed recheck. If nothing is found, surveillance in that area continues at reduced intensity into the next season, since an undetected nest could produce overwintering queens.

So the honest answer is: days-to-weeks for the initial response, then continuous seasonal surveillance — not a discrete "wait, then recheck" interval. This is an empirical judgment about agency practice, not a documented fixed period.

Convincing evidence of eradication is **absence of detections despite adequate surveillance**, not merely absence of reports. Concretely, that means: no confirmed positive ID (and no nest, specimen, or DNA/eDNA trace) anywhere in the state across **at least three consecutive full seasons** — three years is the standard rule of thumb, because it spans the multi-year life cycle and the possibility of an undetected nest producing overwintering queens.

Crucially, the evidence only counts if surveillance effort is maintained at a level sufficient to have detected the hornet had it been present — continued trapping, public reporting, and look-alike screening at roughly the intensity of the active years. Zero detections under weak surveillance proves nothing.

So: roughly **three years of active-season surveillance with no confirmed detection**, under sustained monitoring, is the threshold at which one could credibly declare eradication. This is an empirical judgment based on invasion-biology practice, not a documented Washington standard.

A real spread is signaled by **confirmed positives appearing in new, spatially distinct locations over time** — not by the raw volume of reports rising. Report volume is dominated by reporting effort and seasonal insect activity, so a pile-up of reports alone is noise.

The threshold that feels like real spread: **two or more confirmed positive IDs (or a nest/specimen) separated by more than the queen's ~30 km dispersal range, in different seasons or years**, with the detections persisting rather than being one-off. A single confirmed detection, or multiple positives clustered within a few km, is consistent with one incipient colony, not spread.

So the trigger is **geographically independent confirmations accumulating across seasons**, ideally with the positives not explainable by a single introduction point. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise count.

There is no published figure, so this is an empirical judgment. A state agency like the Washington State Department of Agriculture, running this response with a small dedicated team (a handful of entomologists/inspectors, not a large field force), can realistically do on the order of **a few to roughly 10–20 field visits per week** during the active season.

The binding constraints are staff time and travel, not report volume: each visit costs roughly half a day to a day including travel across a large state, and the same people also run trapping, lab screening, and outreach. So the practical ceiling is set by how many inspector-days per week the agency can spare — typically single digits to low tens — which is far below the thousands of reports received. That gap is exactly why triage/prioritization is necessary.
